ON THE EXPONENTIAL SUM OVER K-FREE NUMBERS
J. Br¨udern, A. Granville1, A. Perelli, R. C. Vaughan2 and T. D. Wooley3
Abstract. This paper is concerned with mean values of exponential sum generating functions over k-
free numbers, and especially their L1-means. We also provide non-trivial estimates for the L2-means of
such generating functions restricted to the minor arcs occurring in Hardy-Littlewood dissections, thereby
permitting the circle method to be successfully applied to certain additive problems hitherto beyond its
reach.
1. Introduction
Applications of the Hardy-Littlewood method to diophantine problems, with variables restricted to
inconvenient sets A, can frequently be much simplified provided that the L1-mean of the exponential
sum generated by Ais suitably small (see §6 for a discussion of this idea). It is therefore a matter of some
interest to determine in what circumstances such L1-means are indeed small. It seems that the only
non-trivial exponential sums whose L1-means have been investigated hitherto are those corresponding
to the von Mangoldt function, Λ, and the M¨obius function, µ. Thus, denoting e2πiz by e(z), Vaughan

Sections 2, 3 and 4 of this paper are devoted to the proof of the upper bound recorded in Theorem 2.
We exploit two observations in this proof. First we make use of the high level of distribution of k-free
numbers amongst arithmetic progressions to gain control of the contribution of the major arcs to the
L2-mean of fk(α). This we achieve in §3 through the use of sums of Barban-Davenport-Halberstam
type, the necessary prerequisites being covered in §2. It transpires that the major arcs in the Hardy-
Littlewood dissection of the L2-mean of fk(α) contribute the leading term in the asymptotic formula
(1.3). Thus a non-trivial estimate for the corresponding minor arc contribution may be obtained by
merely subtracting the major arc contribution from the expression on the right hand side of (1.3). This
second idea we pursue in §4, where we complete the proof of Theorem 2. In §5 we provide brief proofs of
the corollaries to Theorem 2. We turn our attention in §6 to lower bounds for L1-means of exponential
sums, proving Theorem 3 and its corollaries, and also providing a proof of the lower bound in (1.2).
Finally, in §7, we describe an essentially elementary argument which completes the proof of Theorem 1.

item.text: Parry’s fixed-modulus theorem offers a shorter route: sum its explicit error terms, then average its arithmetic main factor over the polynomial values. This appears to give a usable range with moduli above \(x^{7/9}\) and below \(x\) by a fixed power. The numerics also show that a constant-only main term cannot remain uniform when \(f(y)/x\) stays positive.

ON THE EXPONENTIAL SUM OVER K-FREE NUMBERS
J. Br¨udern, A. Granville1, A. Perelli, R. C. Vaughan2 and T. D. Wooley3
Abstract. This paper is concerned with mean values of exponential sum generating functions over k-
free numbers, and especially their L1-means. We also provide non-trivial estimates for the L2-means of
such generating functions restricted to the minor arcs occurring in Hardy-Littlewood dissections, thereby
permitting the circle method to be successfully applied to certain additive problems hitherto beyond its
reach.
1. Introduction
Applications of the Hardy-Littlewood method to diophantine problems, with variables restricted to
inconvenient sets A, can frequently be much simplified provided that the L1-mean of the exponential
sum generated by Ais suitably small (see §6 for a discussion of this idea). It is therefore a matter of some
interest to determine in what circumstances such L1-means are indeed small. It seems that the only
non-trivial exponential sums whose L1-means have been investigated hitherto are those corresponding
to the von Mangoldt function, Λ, and the M¨obius function, µ. Thus, denoting e2πiz by e(z), Vaughan

proposed manner. In the case s= 2, however, their circle method approach fails, and they remark that
“though the analytic method is still applicable in principle, there seems little hope of its furnishing a
practicable proof in this case”. Indeeed, for the binary problem Evelyn and Linfoot were forced to make

over the elementary methods. For example, one can obtain an asymptotic formula for the number of

Sections 2, 3 and 4 of this paper are devoted to the proof of the upper bound recorded in Theorem 2.
We exploit two observations in this proof. First we make use of the high level of distribution of k-free
numbers amongst arithmetic progressions to gain control of the contribution of the major arcs to the
L2-mean of fk(α). This we achieve in §3 through the use of sums of Barban-Davenport-Halberstam
type, the necessary prerequisites being covered in §2. It transpires that the major arcs in the Hardy-
Littlewood dissection of the L2-mean of fk(α) contribute the leading term in the asymptotic formula
(1.3). Thus a non-trivial estimate for the corresponding minor arc contribution may be obtained by
merely subtracting the major arc contribution from the expression on the right hand side of (1.3). This
second idea we pursue in §4, where we complete the proof of Theorem 2. In §5 we provide brief proofs of
the corollaries to Theorem 2. We turn our attention in §6 to lower bounds for L1-means of exponential
sums, proving Theorem 3 and its corollaries, and also providing a proof of the lower bound in (1.2).

Sections 2, 3 and 4 of this paper are devoted to the proof of the upper bound recorded in Theorem 2.
We exploit two observations in this proof. First we make use of the high level of distribution of k-free
numbers amongst arithmetic progressions to gain control of the contribution of the major arcs to the
L2-mean of fk(α). This we achieve in §3 through the use of sums of Barban-Davenport-Halberstam
type, the necessary prerequisites being covered in §2. It transpires that the major arcs in the Hardy-
Littlewood dissection of the L2-mean of fk(α) contribute the leading term in the asymptotic formula
(1.3). Thus a non-trivial estimate for the corresponding minor arc contribution may be obtained by
merely subtracting the major arc contribution from the expression on the right hand side of (1.3). This
second idea we pursue in §4, where we complete the proof of Theorem 2. In §5 we provide brief proofs of
the corollaries to Theorem 2. We turn our attention in §6 to lower bounds for L1-means of exponential
sums, proving Theorem 3 and its corollaries, and also providing a proof of the lower bound in (1.2).
Finally, in §7, we describe an essentially elementary argument which completes the proof of Theorem 1.

Correcting that gives constants near \(0.14\), consistent with the numerical extrapolations. I’ll make the analytic evaluation a separate proposition and use a weaker contour estimate that avoids relying on the paper’s sharper bound.

ARITHMETIC PROGRESSION

J. BRÜDERN AND T. D. WOOLEY*

**ABSTRACT.** An analogue of the Montgomery-Hooley asymptotic formula is established for the variance of the number of primes in arithmetic progressions, in which the moduli are restricted to the values of a polynomial.

## 1. INTRODUCTION

The distribution of primes is a fundamental problem in the theory of numbers. Our concern here is with the error terms that arise in the prime number theorem for arithmetic progressions. Let φ denote Euler’s totient, and define the relevant quantity \(E(x; k, l)\) for real \(x \ge 2\), and coprime natural numbers \(k\) and \(l\), through the equation

\[
\sum_{\substack{p \le x \\ p \equiv l \bmod k}} \log p = \frac{x}{\phi(k)} + E(x; k, l).
\]

Montgomery [8] obtained an asymptotic formula for the variance

\[
V(x, y) = \sum_{k \le y} \sum_{\substack{l=1 \\ (l,k)=1}}^{k} |E(x; k, l)|^2
\]

ON THE EXPONENTIAL SUM OVER K-FREE NUMBERS

J. Brüdern, A. Granville¹, A. Perelli, R. C. Vaughan² and T. D. Wooley³

**Abstract.** This paper is concerned with mean values of exponential sum generating functions over *k*-free numbers, and especially their *L*¹-means. We also provide non-trivial estimates for the *L*²-means of such generating functions restricted to the minor arcs occurring in Hardy-Littlewood dissections, thereby permitting the circle method to be successfully applied to certain additive problems hitherto beyond its reach.

## 1. Introduction

Applications of the Hardy-Littlewood method to diophantine problems, with variables restricted to inconvenient sets 𝒜, can frequently be much simplified provided that the *L*¹-mean of the exponential sum generated by 𝒜 is suitably small (see §6 for a discussion of this idea). It is therefore a matter of some interest to determine in what circumstances such *L*¹-means are indeed small. It seems that the only non-trivial exponential sums whose *L*¹-means have been investigated hitherto are those corresponding to the von Mangoldt function, Λ, and the Möbius function, μ. Thus, denoting e^{2πiz} by e(z), Vaughan (1988) has shown that

x^{1/2} ≪ ∫₀¹ |∑_{1≤n≤x} Λ(n)e(nα)| dα ≤ (1 + o(1))(x log(2x))^{1/2},

and Balog and Perelli (to appear) have very recently established the bounds

exp(c log x / log log x) ≪ ∫₀¹ |∑_{1≤n≤x} μ(n)e(nα)| dα ≪ x^{1/2},

for a suitable positive number c. In each case the upper bounds, which are believed to lie close to the truth, follow from the corresponding *L*²-means via the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. Within the framework of the Hardy-Littlewood method, such a belief implies that a positive proportion of the *L*²-mean must be concentrated on suitably chosen minor arcs. Our primary concern in this paper is to establish bounds for the *L*¹- and *L*²-means of the exponential sum formed with the *k*-free numbers, which is to say the numbers not divisible by any *k*th power of a prime. Our conclusions are in marked contrast with the above cases. When *k* ≥ 2, the *L*¹-mean of this exponential sum is substantially smaller than the bound derived from the *L*²-mean via the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, and the *L*²-mean is concentrated on the major arcs of the Hardy-Littlewood dissection.

In order to describe our first theorem we require some notation. Let μ_k(n) be the characteristic function of the *k*-free numbers, and define f_k(α) = f_k(α; x) by

f_k(α; x) = ∑_{1≤n≤x} μ_k(n)e(nα). (1.1)

SPARSE VARIANCE FOR PRIMES IN  
ARITHMETIC PROGRESSION

J. BRÜDERN AND T. D. WOOLEY*

**ABSTRACT.** An analogue of the Montgomery-Hooley asymptotic formula is established for the variance of the number of primes in arithmetic progressions, in which the moduli are restricted to the values of a polynomial.

## 1. INTRODUCTION

The distribution of primes is a fundamental problem in the theory of numbers. Our concern here is with the error terms that arise in the prime number theorem for arithmetic progressions. Let φ denote Euler’s totient, and define the relevant quantity \(E(x; k, l)\) for real \(x \ge 2\), and coprime natural numbers \(k\) and \(l\), through the equation

\[
\sum_{\substack{p \le x \\ p \equiv l \bmod k}} \log p = \frac{x}{\phi(k)} + E(x; k, l).
\]

Montgomery [8] obtained an asymptotic formula for the variance

\[
V(x, y) = \sum_{k \le y} \sum_{\substack{l=1 \\ (l,k)=1}}^{k} |E(x; k, l)|^2
\]

ON THE EXPONENTIAL SUM OVER K-FREE NUMBERS

J. Brüdern, A. Granville¹, A. Perelli, R. C. Vaughan² and T. D. Wooley³

**Abstract.** This paper is concerned with mean values of exponential sum generating functions over *k*-free numbers, and especially their *L*¹-means. We also provide non-trivial estimates for the *L*²-means of such generating functions restricted to the minor arcs occurring in Hardy-Littlewood dissections, thereby permitting the circle method to be successfully applied to certain additive problems hitherto beyond its reach.

## 1. Introduction

Applications of the Hardy-Littlewood method to diophantine problems, with variables restricted to inconvenient sets 𝒜, can frequently be much simplified provided that the *L*¹-mean of the exponential sum generated by 𝒜 is suitably small (see §6 for a discussion of this idea). It is therefore a matter of some interest to determine in what circumstances such *L*¹-means are indeed small. It seems that the only non-trivial exponential sums whose *L*¹-means have been investigated hitherto are those corresponding to the von Mangoldt function, Λ, and the Möbius function, μ. Thus, denoting e^{2πiz} by e(z), Vaughan (1988) has shown that

x^{1/2} ≪ ∫₀¹ |∑_{1≤n≤x} Λ(n)e(nα)| dα ≤ (1 + o(1))(x log(2x))^{1/2},

and Balog and Perelli (to appear) have very recently established the bounds

exp(c log x / log log x) ≪ ∫₀¹ |∑_{1≤n≤x} μ(n)e(nα)| dα ≪ x^{1/2},

for a suitable positive number c. In each case the upper bounds, which are believed to lie close to the truth, follow from the corresponding *L*²-means via the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. Within the framework of the Hardy-Littlewood method, such a belief implies that a positive proportion of the *L*²-mean must be concentrated on suitably chosen minor arcs. Our primary concern in this paper is to establish bounds for the *L*¹- and *L*²-means of the exponential sum formed with the *k*-free numbers, which is to say the numbers not divisible by any *k*th power of a prime. Our conclusions are in marked contrast with the above cases. When *k* ≥ 2, the *L*¹-mean of this exponential sum is substantially smaller than the bound derived from the *L*²-mean via the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality, and the *L*²-mean is concentrated on the major arcs of the Hardy-Littlewood dissection.

In order to describe our first theorem we require some notation. Let μ_k(n) be the characteristic function of the *k*-free numbers, and define f_k(α) = f_k(α; x) by

f_k(α; x) = ∑_{1≤n≤x} μ_k(n)e(nα). (1.1)

### 1998 Publications

#### On the exponential sum over \( k\)-free numbers (with Joerg Brudern, Alberto Perelli, Bob Vaughan and Trevor Wooley )
Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society, 356 (1998), 739-761.

We give upper and lower bounds for exponential sums over \( k\)-power free numbers

Article

#### A binary additive problem of Erdös and the order of \(2 \pmod {p^2}\) (with K. Soundararajan )
Ramanujan Journal, 2 (1998), 283-298.

We show that the problem of representing every odd integer as the sum of a squarefree number and a power of 2 is strongly related to the problem of showing that \( p^2\) divides \( 2^{p-1}-1\) for few primes \( p\).

Article

#### ABC allows us to can count squarefrees,
International Mathematical Research Notices, 19 (1998), 991-1009.

We show that the \( abc\)-conjecture allows one to give the appropriate estimate for the number of squarefree values of any given polynomial

Article

#### International team shows that primes can be found in surprising places,
Resonance, 3 (1998), 71-72.

A journalistic article on the breakthrough of Friedlander and Iwaniec on primes of the form \( a^2+b^4\)

/bin/zsh -lc "python3 -c 'import math,json
N=1000000
s=bytearray([1])*(N+1);s[:2]=bytes([0,0])
for p in range(2,math.isqrt(N)+1):
 if s[p]:s[p*p::p]=bytes([0])*((N-p*p)//p+1)
P=Mo=Mq=Mc=1
for p in range(2,N+1):
 if not s[p]:continue
 P*=1-2/(p*(p+1))
 a=(math.sqrt(p)-p)/(p*p+p-2);b=(1-math.sqrt(p))/(p*p+p-2)
 if p"'!=2:Mo*=1+a/p+b/(p*p)
 rho=1 if p==2 else (2 if p%4==1 else 0)
 Mq*=1+a*rho/p+b*(0 if p==2 else rho)/(p*p)
 rc=1 if p in (2,3) or p%3==2 else (3 if pow(p-2,(p-1)//3,p)==1 else 0)
 Mc*=1+a*rc/p+b*(0 if p in (2,3) else rc)/(p*p)
K=-4*(-.20788622497735457)/(math.pi**2/6)*P
print("prime cutoff",N,"kappa",K,"C odd",2*K*Mo/3,"C quadratic",2*K*Mq/3,"C cubic",2*K*Mc/3)
d=json.load(open("results.json"))
for key,v in d["polynomials"].items():
 mx=max(row["x"] for row in v["rows"])
 rr=[row for row in v["normalised"] if row["x"]==mx]
 print(key,"largest x",mx,"N at r=.01 and 1",[(r["ratio"],r["V_over_x12_fy32_at_nominal_ratio"]) for r in rr if r["ratio"] in (.01,1)])'"'"

Reconstruct a fixed-modulus variance estimate, then average its multiplicative main factor over polynomial values. The resulting asymptotic range is x^(7/9+δ) ≤ f(y) ≤ x^(1−δ), for fixed 0 < δ < 1/9. The main analytic proposition uses a weaker contour estimate than the supplied fixed-modulus paper. That paper cannot be applied verbatim: its residue computation omits the factor 1/2 from ζ(2s+2), doubling its squarefree constant, and its displayed Euler product for ζ(−1/2) requires analytic continuation. The corrected prediction agrees with the numerical extrapolations. Restricting to integer coefficients ensures that polynomial congruences have period equal to their modulus and satisfy the Chinese remainder theorem without denominator corrections. Reviewed sources: J. Brüdern and T. D. Wooley, Sparse variance for primes in arithmetic progression (2011), https://doi.org/10.1093/qmath/hap029, used for motivation only; J. Brüdern, A. Granville, A. Perelli, R. C. Vaughan and T. D. Wooley, On the exponential sum over k-free numbers (1998), https://doi.org/10.1098/rsta.1998.0183; Tomos Parry, A variance for k-free numbers in arithmetic progressions of given modulus (2019, revised 2023), arXiv:1912.04683v2. Neither excluded source was searched, opened, or used.",
  "main_theorem": "Let f ∈ Z[t] have degree d ≥ 1 and satisfy the assumptions in problem.md. All prime products below run over positive primes. Let ζ denote the analytically continued Riemann zeta function. Define A_p = (p²−2+√p)/(p²+p−2), B_p = (p²−1)/(p²+p−2), κ = −4ζ(−1/2)ζ(2)^(−1) ∏_p(1−2/(p(p+1))), and C(f) = (2κ/3)∏_p[1+(A_p−1)ρ(p)/p+(B_p−A_p)ρ(p²)/p²]. These products converge absolutely and C(f) > 0. For every 0 < ε < 1/(4d), there exists K(f,ε) such that, uniformly for real x ≥ 2 and y ≥ 1 with Y = f(y) ≤ x, |V_f(x,y)−C(f)x^(1/2)Y^(3/2)| ≤ K(f,ε)[x^(4/9+ε)Y^(14/9)+x^(5/3+ε)log(2Y)+x^(1/2)Y^(3/2−1/(2d)+ε)]. Consequently, for every fixed 0 < δ < 1/9 there exists K(f,δ) such that, uniformly when x^(7/9+δ) ≤ Y ≤ x^(1−δ), |V_f(x,y)/(C(f)x^(1/2)Y^(3/2))−1| ≤ K(f,δ)x^(−δ/(100d)).",
